newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bourse watchdog probes Cerus leaks.
newsitem.headline: French bourse watchdog probes Cerus leaks.

text.p: The Paris stockmarket's regulator COB announced on Wednesday that it was investigating leaks of a proposed buyout plan of Italian businessman Carlo De Benedetti's French holding company Cerus.

The leaks, published on Monday and Tuesday in the French newspaper Les Echos, spurred heavy buying in shares of Cerus and car parts maker Valeo until the buyout plan was denied at mid-morning on Tuesday by reported bidder CGIP.
The denial sent the shares into a tailspin and led to several trading suspensions, infuriating traders who felt duped.
"Don't they read the papers at CGIP? They waited until midday to deny this report? Look at these trading volumes," one trader said.
Weekly financial newsletter La Lettre de l'Expansion also ran an item on Monday saying CGIP was interested in Cerus.

The COB (Commission des operations de bourse), which has grown more aggressive in policing the bourse in recent months, said on Wednesday that it had opened an investigation and notified the people concerned.

"In view of the information published in the last few days concerning a possible buyout by CGIP of Cerus and Valeo, the COB has decided to open an inquiry as required by its rules on the disclosure of information," a COB spokeswoman told Reuters.

Les Echos on Wednesday quoted CGIP chairman Ernest-Antoine Seilliere as saying he was still interested in Cerus's 28 percent stake in Valeo, a thriving car parts supplier whose future lies at the heart of an eight-month takeover saga.
De Benedetti has been looking for a buyer since last February, but French authorities and the French car industry insist Valeo must be under French ownership.

Analysts say the problem is that no French company appears willing or able to pay the 20 billion franc ($3.90 billion) or more to acquire Valeo, and most negotiations are aiming for transactions that would avoid a public offer.
Under French bourse rules, a takeover bid is not required if less than a third of the capital changes hands. Cerus holds 28 percent of the capital, but 42 percent of the voting rights.
The extra rights would not pass to a new owner, so a buyer of Cerus's stake does not seem legally obliged to launch a bid.
Seilliere said a buyout of Valeo was out of CGIP's reach. He and De Benedetti are discussing their options and will put them to their respective boards in early October.
Analysts say they suspect bourse regulators are watching this case closely to ensure the interests of Valeo's other shareholders are protected in any deal.
"They're aware that if they ride roughshod over the majority shareholders, it'll reflect on the Paris bourse, and they're trying to compete internationally," a French analyst said.

Separately, a COB working committee issued a report on Wednesday on the protection of minority shareholders. It advocated public offers whenever a merger occurs, and regulatory clearance beforehand to dispel any uncertainty.

The COB opened 86 investigations in 1995, down from 91 in 1994, but the number of cases passed on for judicial action rose to 25 from 23. The sanctions proceedings also rose to 14 from 12, the regulator said in April.
